segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Wards in Chancery

utterances.text: I'm your host, and each week we step into the fog of Charles Dickens's masterpiece—line by line, passage by passage—to uncover how this novel still grips us, nearly two centuries later.
Not just mood or setting—but the very air the characters breathe.
We're joined by three brilliant readers whose minds work in different orbits, but whose love for this novel burns bright.
Sarah Chen is a computational linguist who studies how sentence structure shapes what we feel—especially when language begins to break down.
Rebecca Martinez is an observational astronomer who brings the rigor of data and scale to literary patterns—looking for constellations in the text.
And Elena Volkov is a musicologist and cultural historian who hears the rhythms of power and resistance in Dickens's prose.
Sarah, before we do anything else—can you read us the opening fog passage?
But I want you to do it the way you'd do it to prove a point to a skeptic.
Read it so we can actually feel what you're describing about the syntax.
I’ll read the first paragraph of the novel—the fog over London Bridge.
Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights.

Fog creeping into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and steeples, and hovering about the chimneys of great ships; fog down in the hole of the Basin Plan; fog in the eyes and throats of ancient Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper, down in his close cabin; fog, fog, fog.
All the influence of the earth, all the clatter of the teeming city, all the power of the bloodless cold that holds it, seems concentrated into a heap of mud in the streets.
The raw afternoon is rawest, the dense fog is densest, the muddy streets are muddiest, without any countervailing good.”
The fog operates at one scale.
Rebecca, you said something in our pre-chat that I keep coming back to—
that Bleak House the house and Chancery aren't really in conflict.
They're just operating at different scales simultaneously.
Dickens clearly wants us to feel the warmth of that dinner scene as a rebuke to the fog.
Are you saying that's an illusion?
Think of it like a microclimate.
You can have a warm room in a frozen city.
But it doesn’t change the weather.
With respect, I think that undersells it.
Bleak House isn’t just a warm room.
Let me read you the passage where Esther first arrives.

“Such, with its illuminated windows, softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.”
Elena, I suspect you want to come back at that.
and I don't think you mean it as a comfort or an escape hatch.
What is Bleak House doing politically that Rebecca's reading might be underselling?
When Elena talks about two temporalities.
Or Rebecca talks about nested systems.
Are those just sophisticated ways of describing what the grammar is already doing?
Sarah, here's a question you might find annoying—
when Elena talks about 'two temporalities' or Rebecca talks about 'nested systems,'
are those just sophisticated ways of describing what the grammar is already doing?
I mean, is the argument in the ideas, or is it actually baked into the sentences in a way that doesn't require us to go outside the text at all?
The fog passage doesn’t just describe paralysis.
The same thing happens in the Chancery vacation passage.
“The good ships Law and Equity, those teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened, brazen-faced, and not by any means fast-sailing clippers are laid up in ordinary.”
I don’t disagree with the syntax.
But the ship metaphor tells us something else.
It’s not just that they’re idle.
The system is built for motion.
You called his speech the emotional and political heart of the novel.
Can you read us that line—'Of all my old associations...'—
and then tell me: is Gridley a tragic figure, or is he actually Dickens's model of how you're supposed to fight back?
“Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for.
There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!”
But in that final declaration, he names what survives.
it’s the only variable that doesn’t scale.
“Of all my old associations… of all my old pursuits… of all the living and the dead world…”
Syntax, scale, and solidarity—all meeting in one line.
Next time, we’ll follow that thread into the unraveling of Richard Carstone.
And the slow erosion of a mind.

segments.title: Deep Dive: Richard's UnravelingAmbition and Law

utterances.text: We've seen how Chancery casts its fog over the lives of the wardens and how the system distorts time, perception, memory.
Now we turn to one of its most tragic casualties Richard Carstone.
Sarah, you've flagged something I want to start with because it's the kind of thing most readers just glide past.

In that c23:p37 passage 'I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow, if I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on...' you're saying that repetition isn't just Richard being selfpitying, it's actually doing something linguistically specific.
What exactly is Dickens capturing there, and does it tell us something about Richard that a purely thematic reading would miss?
Yes and it's not just repetition.
It's recursive syntax a structure that folds back on itself.
Richard says: 'I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow.'
I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow
Then he repeats it: 'If I were a more constant sort of fellow...'
If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death
No future action, no past closure.
Just a mind circling a failure it can't exit.
And that loop isn't psychological it's structural.
He's being failed by a system that dangles inheritance like a tether but never lets him grasp it.
Chancery doesn't just delay justice it dissolves agency.
Elena, you've said something that I find genuinely provocative
That Richard isn't inconstant by nature, he's being *made* inconstant by the institution.
So when he says 'I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow,' he's actually misdiagnosing himself.
But doesn't that let Richard off the hook entirely?
Where does personal agency end and systemic destruction begin in your reading?
It doesn't let him off the hook it relocates the hook.
The failure isn't moral it's institutional.
I wonder if we're describing different phases of the same process.
Elena sees structure I see trajectory.
Richard isn't just being acted upon.
He has what I'd call a constitutional instability from the start.
Like a star with too little mass to sustain fusion.
Rebecca, you want to read that passage in c13:p124 'so they passed away into the shadow and were gone' as something like stellar death, a slow dimming rather than a catastrophic collapse.
But Elena is sitting here saying that shadow is institutional, it's Chancery's atmosphere colonizing private life.
Are you two actually describing the same thing from different angles, or is there a real disagreement about what's causing Richard's trajectory?
In c13:p124, the sun is shining as they walk through the room.
So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over.
It's not that the shadow was always there.
It's that their passage triggers it.
And it's not that they trigger it they're stepping into it.
And linguistically, the sentence structure supports both readings.
Look at the main clause: 'they passed away into the shadow.'
But then the next sentence shifts agency: 'It was only a burst of light...'
Sarah, you mentioned something in our preconversation that I keep coming back to:

That in c51:p64, the death scene, Ada grammatically takes the main verb she's the one kneeling, clasping, turning while Richard is syntactically backgrounded, almost dissolved into participial phrases.
Does that mean Dickens is encoding something about agency and personhood in the clause structure itself?
Because that's a wild claim and I want to make sure I'm understanding it right.
The main clause begins: 'my darling rose...'
Then the rest is a cascade of participles: 'putting off,' 'kneeling,' 'clasping,' 'turning.'
Richard is the object of prepositions: 'beside him,' 'on his head,' 'round his neck.'
And that's the moment before the event horizon.
Rebecca, you said Ada's golden hair falling on Richard's dying head in c51:p64 isn't redemption
It's the last light before total darkness, the moment before something crosses the event horizon and disappears forever.
Elena would say that's actually beautiful but also part of the problem that love becomes a sedative, a private consolation that makes institutional destruction almost bearable.
Is Ada's love in that scene something Dickens wants us to find comfort in, or is he indicting it?
And it's weaponized by the narrative to soften the indictment.
We're made to weep for Ada not to rage at Chancery.
It tells us how close we are to the collapse.
Richard is reduced to a series of prepositional phrases.
And so we see how love, language, and law entangle in ways that both reveal and obscure.
Next, we'll turn to another kind of concealment one buried not in syntax, but in blood and silence.

segments.title: The Architecture of Secrecy: Lady Dedlock's Buried Past

utterances.text: We've just left Richard adrift in the fog of Chancery.
Now let's turn to a different kind of unraveling—one held taut beneath a powdered wig and a diamond stomacher.
Rebecca, you described Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn as particles locked in orbit around each other—which is a wild and kind of beautiful way to read a Victorian drawing room.
But I want to push on something.
You said the secrecy is a condition they inhabit, not a choice.
Elena would say it's a condition that was imposed specifically on Lady Dedlock—that the social system engineered her vulnerability.
And that calling it 'cosmic' or 'eternal' actually lets the system off the hook.
Does the astronomy framing risk aestheticizing something that's really just institutional cruelty?
But I don’t mean ‘cosmic’ as romantic.
They’re not free to exit the orbit.
But because the field itself won’t allow it.
Tulkinghorn can’t reveal what he knows.
And the system—that web of class, law, silence—produces that lock.
But let’s name what’s being baked.
Lady Dedlock’s secret isn’t just hers.
It belongs to the Dedlock name.
He’s not some neutral force of nature.
And he chooses when to rattle them.
Sarah, you said you want to actually read that long conditional passage aloud—the 'but whether each evermore watches' sequence.
Because the syntax performs the unresolvability.
And then tell me: is Dickens being linguistically precise, or is he just a brilliant impressionist who stumbled into something that looks like linguistics?
Let’s take the moment after Tulkinghorn delivers his news.

During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject...
But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation...
Whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares...
What each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.
No main verb ever claims them.
And the final clause—'what each would give'—isn’t even syntactically coordinated.
Dickens knew exactly what he was doing.
But the effect—the suspended uncertainty—is what matters.
It mirrors the state of not knowing.
Like waiting for a star to go supernova.
Elena, you flagged a line about Tulkinghorn—he 'carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress' and is 'his own client in that matter.'
You said he becomes the institution.
But Sarah's reading suggests he's actually the most linguistically powerful person in every room.
Is Tulkinghorn a victim of the system, or is he the system's most willing architect?
Because I think you two might actually disagree about whether he has any interiority left at all.
And that line—'he carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress'—
He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.
The secrets have replaced his organs.
But look at how he speaks.
He wields power by becoming a non-person.
Like a KGB archivist in 1970s Kyiv.
The less you are, the more dangerous you become.
Elena, you said the real horror isn't Lady Dedlock's secret—it's that the price of existing in this world is permanent self-erasure.
But there's that line: 'Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.'
Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.
Is Dickens sympathizing with her, or is he slightly mocking the performance she's trapped in?
Because Rebecca might say the irony is the point—it's what makes the suffering cosmic rather than pathetic.
The satire doesn’t cancel the tragedy.
She’s trapped in a role so absurd it’s unbearable.
And that awareness—that she’s performing a myth she no longer believes—
But because the condition persists beyond any single life.
Rebecca, you said something that stuck with me—that the most terrifying thing about hidden knowledge isn't discovery.
It’s the possibility it might never be discovered.
And you spend your life frozen.
Growing up in the desert gave you a feel for that kind of isolating vastness.
Does Dickens's drawing room actually feel that way to you?
And—Sarah, Elena—does that land for you, or does the domestic setting make that kind of cosmic loneliness feel like a stretch?
The silence in that room—the way they watch each other—it’s like standing in a canyon and knowing your voice won’t echo.
I’d say the compression makes it more intense.
And that pressure chamber is the state.
So secrecy isn’t just a plot device.
And the people inside it—Lady Dedlock, Tulkinghorn, even Sir Leicester—are its prisoners and its keepers.
Next, we’ll look at someone with no power at all.
A child who can’t even claim a name.

segments.title: Jo and the Machinery of Indifference: Social Critique in Bleak House

utterances.text: We’ve just left Lady Dedlock trembling under the weight of a secret, held in place by one man’s cold authority.
Now let’s turn to someone with no authority at all—no name, no home, no witness.
Sarah, you made this claim in our pre-chat that stopped me cold—
you said Jo doesn’t just sound powerless, he’s literally grammatically prohibited from owning his own speech.
Can you read us that passage from chapter eleven and show us what you mean?
Because I think most people hear ‘He wos wery good to me’ and think Dickens is being sentimental.
You’re saying something much stranger than that.
It begins with the narrator directly addressing Jo:
“Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness, who ‘can’t exactly say’ what will be done to him in greater hands than men’s, thou art not quite in outer darkness.”
The narrator speaks *to* Jo in biblical cadence—archaic, dignified.
“There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: ‘He wos wery good to me, he wos!’”
The quote is embedded in the narrator’s sentence.
It’s ‘in thy muttered reason for this’—the grammar subordinates Jo’s voice to the narrator’s judgment.
His speech is *muttered*. It’s not declared. It’s not his own.
The system doesn’t just fail to hear Jo.
It requires him to be unheard.
Host, you asked me about Tom-all-Alone’s.
Let me read this from c22:p51.

“When they come at last to Tom-all-Alone’s, Mr. Bucket stops for a moment at the corner and takes a lighted bull’s-eye from the constable on duty there, who then accompanies him with his own particular bull’s-eye at his waist.”

“Between his two conductors, Mr. Snagsby passes along the middle of a villainous street, undrained, unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water—though the roads are dry elsewhere—and reeking with such smells and sights that he, who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses.”
That clause—'though the roads are dry elsewhere'—
But let’s look at the moment in c11:p87—

“That one cold winter night when he, the boy, was shivering in a doorway near his crossing, the man turned to look at him, and came back, and having questioned him and found that he had not a friend in the world, said, ‘Neither have I. Not one!’ and gave him the price of a supper and a night’s lodging.”
Two beings recognize each other in the dark.
But the novel doesn’t let us rest there.

“Lady Dedlock, have the goodness to stop and hear me, or before you reach the staircase I shall ring the alarm-bell and rouse the house. And then I must speak out before every guest and servant, every man and woman, in it.”
Power doesn’t need to be loud.
It just needs to be absolute.
Rebecca, I want to push you a little here.
You described that moment—the cold night, the man turning to look at the shivering boy, sharing his supper—as cosmology rather than social critique.
But Elena is basically sitting here saying: Dickens is colder than that.
He’s not offering us that moment as comfort.
He’s showing us that the system sees that grace and discards it anyway.
Does the astronomy metaphor hold up against that reading?
Or does it soften something Dickens intends to be brutal?
In astronomy, we detect signals that are overwhelmed by noise.
A faint star in a bright field.
We don’t claim the noise isn’t there.
We claim the signal is real despite it.
But the signal is still sent.
Elena, let’s talk about Mrs. Piper for a second.
All three of you flagged that passage.
You’re saying her testimony shows how rumor gets weaponized by systems—narrative as institutional tool.
But Sarah is saying her sentences literally don’t work—they fail grammatically.
Or are you actually disagreeing about where the damage happens—in the structure of power or in the structure of language?
Language is the first site of control.
Mrs. Piper’s testimony is a hall of mirrors.
She speaks in parentheses, without punctuation, in rambling chains.
“the plaintive—so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased—was reported to have sold himself.”
She distances herself at every turn.
It was *reported*. She *insists*. *Thinks* it was the air.
The grammar of rumor is the grammar of plausible deniability.
And that’s where the linguistic damage is done.
Her sentences have no finite verbs.
It’s the formal erasure of agency.
Last one—and I want all three of you on this.
Sarah, you said the fog passage has no main finite verb for three paragraphs.
And that is the experience of confusion, not a symbol for it.
Rebecca, you’d probably say the atmosphere is doing something closer to spectroscopy—reading social anatomy.
Elena, you’d say the fog is a political choice, like the dry roads.
Are you all describing the same machinery from different angles?
Or is there a real disagreement here about what Dickens thought literature was actually for?
So the fog is not just atmosphere.
And the novel is not just a story.
One we’re all now part of.
Next, we’ll ask what this trial demands of us.
What does it mean to live in a world where dust settles on everything—and everyone?

segments.title: Themes of Entropy and Dust: What the Novel Asks of Us

utterances.text: We've just seen how Jo is caught in a machinery of indifference.
But that machinery doesn’t operate in isolation.
It’s part of a larger system—one that seems to run on decay itself.
Rebecca, you've talked about Dickens using atmosphere not as backdrop but as actual argument—the fog, the bad air, the candlelight going yellow.
But I want to push on something.
Is the novel ultimately pessimistic about all this?
Like, is Dickens saying these systems of entropy *can't* be fixed, they can only be walked away from?
Or is he still leaving a door open somewhere?
I think Dickens is showing us a closed system.
Not just socially closed—legally, thermodynamically closed.
Take the description of Nemo’s room in chapter ten.
Foul and filthy as the room is, foul and filthy as the air is, it is not easy to perceive what fumes those are which most oppress the senses in it
The air is so uniformly degraded that you can’t isolate the source.
through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer’s mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium
The lawyer doesn’t smell it—he *tastes* it in his own mouth.
The system has breached the boundary.
And that’s why I think the answer is no—there’s no door.
It succeeds at what it’s designed to do.
I want to push back slightly on the idea of closure.
Because what we’re seeing isn’t just thematic entropy.
It is nothing to you or to any one else that the great lights of the parliamentary sky have failed for some few years in this business to set you the example of moving on.
It’s *compensating* for its lack of logic with length.
It’s piling up clauses to mask the absurdity of its conclusion.
The one grand recipe remains for you—the profound philosophical prescription—the be-all and the end-all of your strange existence upon earth.
Each more inflated than the last.
The command ‘Move on’ isn’t a directive.
Like the Soviet composers’ union telling a dissident to ‘re-educate’.
But the form is total control.
And that’s why I find it so chilling when the narrator says—
You are by no means to move off, Jo, for the great lights can’t at all agree about that.
They won’t even let him leave.
It’s about maintaining the appearance of doing something.
The system is feeding on its own noise.
And that brings me to Tulkinghorn.
Because he embodies that same principle.
As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case.
The case is all there is.
The simile doesn’t just compare Tulkinghorn to a case.
We only hear about the impossibility of hearing it.
The sentence denies the existence of an inner self.
But I’d argue the metaphor works precisely because it preserves the *idea* of an inner tone.
We infer its presence by gravitational effects.
It’s a vacuum that pulls everything in.
Elena, you’ve compared Dickens’s institutions to Soviet systems.
But here’s what I want to test: Esther.
Is that *resistance* to the machine, or has she just internalized exactly what the machine wants from people it can use?
Esther performs the role the system rewards.
But in doing so, she creates a space of care.
Look at how she responds to Ada and Richard.
They went on in their own wild way for a little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself

how it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other’s sake.
On endurance as an act of will.
But I keep coming back to cost.
What does it extract from her?
The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself.
She makes emotional business for itself.
She sustains the system by being what it can’t replace.
But linguistically, the key is in what’s suppressed.
She says ‘I enjoyed it too much myself’—
I enjoyed it too much myself
That’s the only time she names her own desire.
And even then, it’s framed as excess.
So is constancy a form of resistance—or is it simply what the machine requires to keep turning?
We’ll take that question—and Esther’s silence—with us into our next segment.
Where we’ll look closely at Dickens’s digressive genius—and how form and feeling shape one another in this extraordinary novel.

segments.title: Close Reading: Dickens's Digressive GeniusForm and Feeling

utterances.text: Last time, we walked through the novel's pervasive dust and decayas symptoms of a world slowly collapsing under institutional inertia.
Now, let's look more closely at how Dickens constructs that worldthrough syntax, metaphor, and narrative rhythm.
Rebecca, you said before we started that the fog opening reads to you like a protoplanetary diskprimordial material before any order forms.
Can you just read that first passage aloud and tell us what you're actually hearing when Dickens writes 'as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth'?
Because that's a strange thing for a novelist to reach for.

As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.
What I hear is deep time.
But a kind of cosmological reset.
Sarah, I could hear you tensing up just nowbecause Rebecca just called that passage 'not metaphorical decoration'.
And you've been very clear that what Dickens is doing there is grammatical, not imagistic.
What is actually happening to the sentence when Dickens writes that opening?
There is no main verb in that first sentence.
It mirrors the world it describes.
Elena, you've described that fog passage as functioning like propagandamaking the system look inevitable, geological, not man-made.
But Sarah is saying the grammar is the argument, and Rebecca is saying it's about entropy and physics.
Are any of you actually disagreeing, or are you all describing the same thing from different angles?
so we stop asking who built it.
But natural systems can still be studied.
We don’t need to assign blame
Let me put it this way.
The sentence doesn’t just describe fog.
Elena, you said something in our pre-chat that stopped me coldthat Richard doesn't fail Chancery, Chancery colonizes him so thoroughly that he internalizes its logic and starts blaming himself.
Can you read the 'unfinished house' speech from chapter twenty-three and show us where that happens?
Where does it tip from description into self-indictment?

If you lived in an unfinished house, you couldn’t settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to anything; and yet that’s my unhappy case. I was born into this unfinished contention with all its chances and changes, and it began to unsettle me before I quite knew the difference between a suit at law and a suit of clothes; and it has gone on unsettling me ever since; and here I am now, conscious sometimes that I am but a worthless fellow to love my confiding cousin Ada.
Then he says 'here I am now'.
Sarah, you said Richard's speech is a *performance*that he's using conditional logic and self-deprecation to manage how he looks while he apologizes.
But Elena just read that passage as a man who's genuinely been broken.
Can those both be true at once, or does your linguistic reading actually push back on the idea that he's a victim?
They can be true at once.
I think of it as an unstable system.
Not unlike a star in gravitational collapse.
The forces act on the individual.
Sarah, that passage where they find his remains—'Oh, horror, he IS here!'can you unpack how that line works?
Is it the capitalization doing the screaming?
The capitalization of 'IS' is typographic shouting.
Miss Flite’s story—how Chancery destroyed her familyshows us the same process in slow motion.
Each member drawn deeper, until only wreckage remains.

First, our father was drawn—slowly. Home was drawn with him. In a few years he was a fierce, sour, angry bankrupt without a kind word or a kind look for any one. He had been so different, Fitz Jarndyce. He was drawn to a debtors’ prison. There he died. Then our brother was drawn—swiftly—to drunkenness. And rags. And death. Then my sister was drawn. Hush! Never ask to what! Then I was ill and in misery, and heard, as I had often heard before, that this was all the work of Chancery.
The repetition of 'drawn' becomes a funeral drumbeat.
Each 'drawn' pulls another life into the void.
So Chancery doesn’t just delay justice.
And next time, we’ll ask whether any redemption survives that processor if, like Richard, we carry the system’s failure within us, can we ever truly be free?

segments.title: Closing: The Redemption That Remains Incomplete

utterances.text: We've just been tracing Dickens's formal daring—his digressions, rhythms, the way he lets narrative spiral.
But now, let’s turn to what those forms carry: the slow, irreversible erosion of Richard Carstone.
Sarah, you said something in our chat beforehand that really stuck with me—
that by chapter 17, Dickens has made redemption syntactically impossible for Richard.
Can you walk us through what you mean?
Like, what does it actually look like on the page when grammar deletes a person's agency?
In chapter 17, Mrs. Badger says Richard 'feels languid about the profession.'
He has not that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation.
The grammar gives him no agentive structure.
But isn’t the tragedy also structural?
He’s caught in a system that dangles purpose—
If agency were truly gone by chapter 17,
we’d expect no volitional verbs in Richard’s speech from that point.
But he still says 'I will' and 'I must.'
So the grammar hasn’t fully evacuated agency.
Elena, you called Jarndyce a 'compassionate bureaucrat'—
someone who treats individuals kindly while the machine keeps running.
But isn't there a case that his counsel in chapter 13—
'trust in nothing but Providence and your own efforts'—
But he doesn’t dismantle the machine that’s grinding Richard down.
that's not the one Richard inhabits.
Rebecca, you said Jarndyce’s 'if you DO change' passage is actually cosmic resignation.
But when I read it, it sounds tender.
Is it tragic or is it tender?
Let’s look at the modal structure.
if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins—
It assumes change is not just possible.
And he gives them permission to fail.
The subjunctive 'if you DO change' doesn’t open a possibility.
'never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner.'
Elena thinks it’s Jarndyce telling Richard to operate outside institutional logic.
Rebecca thinks it’s Dickens articulating something like natural law.
You think the incompleteness is the point.
Or is the ambiguity doing the work?
The heathen waggoner appears and vanishes.
The grammar refuses to stabilize meaning.
But I think the waggoner is clear.
He’s the one who trusts only Providence.
Jarndyce is saying: don’t be that man.
I see it as a physical law.
You can’t have motion without both force and direction.
Last one, and I want all three of you on this.
Elena, you said the incompleteness of the redemption is the point.
That Dickens is showing us the system won’t change.
